text:
The fix is in place. Let me verify the logic against all the cases:

- **`is_leap(1900)`**: divisible by 4, but divisible by 100 and not by 400 → `False` ✓ (so Feb 1900 has 28 days, `days_between("1900-02-28", "1900-03-01")` = 1)
- **`is_leap(2100)`**: divisible by 100, not by 400 → `False` ✓ (same fix for 2100)
- **`is_leap(2000)`**: divisible by 400 → `True` ✓ (still a leap year)
- **`is_leap(2024)`**: divisible by 4, not a century year → `True` ✓ (Feb 2024 still has 29 days, so `"2024-02-28"` → `"2024-03-01"` = 2)

The root cause was that `is_leap` only checked `year % 4 == 0`, ignoring the Gregorian century exception, so 1900 and 2100 were treated as leap years, inflating February and shifting all ordinals by one day. The fix restores the full rule: divisible by 4, except century years must also be divisible by 400 — matching the behavior the docstring already documented. This also makes `parse_date` correctly reject `1900-02-29` and accept `2000-02-29`.

The change is a single line in `isodate/dates.py`, no new dependencies, and the existing tests (`test_same_month`, `test_leap_february`, `test_century_february`) all pass with this logic.
